title: Polar decomposition
subtitle: G2 lecture 037000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Stretch first, then place the result
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 037000 · Stretch first, then place the result
slides.lead: Polar decomposition separates a linear map into a positive stretch and a partial isometry.
body: The modulus |A| = (A* A)^{1/2} already tells us how much A stretches each input direction. What remains is to restore the output direction information in a length-preserving way wherever there is nonzero output to preserve.
This yields the factorization A = U|A|, where U is a partial isometry.
slides.takeaway: Polar decomposition is the canonical separation of amount-of-stretch from direction-of-output.

slides.title: Review the modulus
slides.lead: The construction begins with the positive operator |A| on the source space.
body: The norm identity says that |A| already accounts for all length changes caused by A. Therefore any remaining factor should preserve lengths on the subspace where |A| is nonzero.
The kernel of |A| equals the kernel of A, so the directions annihilated by A are already completely identified before U is defined.
slides.takeaway: The modulus determines both the stretching data and the null directions of A.

slides.title: Define U on the range of |A|
slides.lead: The obvious formula is to tell U what to do to a vector of the form |A|x.
body: This says: first recover which input x produced the stretched vector |A|x, then send it to the actual output Ax. If the rule is well defined, it will satisfy U|A| = A by construction.
So the main work is to prove that the output does not depend on which x we use to represent a point of ran|A|.
slides.takeaway: The polar factor is forced on the range of the modulus.

slides.title: Why this rule is well defined
slides.lead: Suppose |A|x = |A|y. Then x − y lies in the kernel of |A|.
body: Because ker|A| = ker A, the difference x − y also lies in ker A. Hence Ax = Ay. Therefore the formula U(|A|x)=Ax does not depend on the chosen representative x.
Linearity follows immediately because both A and |A| are linear. So U is a linear map from ran|A| into the target space.
slides.takeaway: Equality of kernels is exactly what makes the defining rule unambiguous.

slides.title: Why U preserves lengths there
slides.lead: On ran|A|, the map U is length preserving.
body: The norm identity for the modulus shows that U does not add or remove any further stretching on the surviving part of the space. It only changes direction.
Thus U is an isometry from ran|A| onto ran A. In finite dimensions, ran|A| = (ker A)^⊥, so the support of the isometry is exactly the orthogonal complement of the kernel.
slides.takeaway: On the support of A, the polar factor is pure motion with no extra stretching.

slides.title: Extend by zero on the kernel
slides.lead: Define U to vanish on ker A and keep the isometry on (ker A)^⊥.
body: This produces a linear map on the whole source space. It is not an isometry everywhere, because kernel vectors are sent to zero. But it is an isometry on the initial space (ker A)^⊥.
That is exactly what the phrase partial isometry means: isometric on one subspace, zero on its orthogonal complement.
slides.takeaway: The canonical polar factor is a partial isometry, not necessarily a full unitary map.

slides.title: A concrete example
slides.lead: For A(x,y) = (2y,0), the modulus stretches the vertical direction and the polar factor places it on the horizontal axis.
body: The modulus kills the horizontal axis and doubles the vertical axis. The partial isometry U then sends the stretched vertical direction to the horizontal output direction and kills the kernel direction.
Composing them gives exactly A. This example makes the slogan literal: |A| stretches, U places.
slides.takeaway: In examples, the modulus and the polar factor play visibly different geometric roles.

slides.title: Relation to the singular-value decomposition
slides.lead: If A = Σ σ_i u_i v_i^*, then |A| acts by σ_i on v_i and U sends v_i to u_i for positive singular values.
body: Thus the SVD already contains the polar decomposition. The positive operator is |A| = Σ σ_i v_i v_i^*, while the polar factor is the partial isometry Σ_{σ_i>0} u_i v_i^* on the support.
The advantage of the polar decomposition is that it is canonical even when singular vectors inside repeated singular-value spaces are not uniquely chosen.
slides.takeaway: Polar decomposition is the invariant core hidden inside the SVD.

slides.title: When U becomes unitary or orthogonal
slides.lead: If A is injective on a square space, the polar factor preserves lengths on the whole space.
body: When ker A = {0}, the initial space of the partial isometry is the entire domain, so U becomes an isometry everywhere. If, in addition, the domain and codomain have the same finite dimension, that isometry is unitary in the complex case or orthogonal in the real case.
So invertible matrices factor as a unitary or orthogonal motion followed by a positive stretching operator.
slides.takeaway: For invertible square matrices, polar decomposition is the operator analogue of magnitude times phase.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: Reconstruct the proof from four steps.
body: First define |A| = (A* A)^{1/2}. Second define U on ran|A| by U(|A|x)=Ax. Third prove this is well defined and isometric there using ker|A|=ker A and |||A|x||=||Ax||. Fourth extend U by zero on ker A. Then A = U|A|.
Those steps are the whole polar decomposition argument in finite dimensions.
slides.takeaway: Well definedness, isometry on the support, and zero extension are the proof skeleton.
